opus-5.5.text:
I don't see them as opposites, though people sometimes frame it that way. Traditional robotics, meaning control theory, motion planning, state estimation, and kinematics and dynamics, gave us a very rigorous foundation. If you know the model of your system and your environment well, those methods are extremely powerful. Look at industrial arms in factories, or the locomotion work from groups like Boston Dynamics. A lot of that is beautifully engineered model-based control.

The problem is that the real world, especially unstructured environments like homes, is messy. You can't write down an accurate model for every object, every deformable cloth, every cluttered kitchen counter. The number of situations explodes, and hand-engineering each one doesn't scale. That's where learning comes in. Learning lets us capture the parts of the problem that are hard to model explicitly: perception, contact-rich manipulation, the long tail of variations, and even human preferences and intent.

So I think of robot learning as extending the reach of robotics rather than replacing it. In my own work, especially early on, I was interested in combining the two: using learning for the things that are hard to specify, while keeping structure for things like planning, task decomposition, and compositional reasoning. A robot doing a long-horizon task, like cooking a meal, needs to reason about sequences of subgoals, and that kind of structure is something classical planning thinks about very carefully.

Now the field has swung quite strongly toward large-scale, end-to-end learning, with large behavior models and vision-language-action models trained on lots of demonstration data. I think that's exciting and has shown real progress. But I'd caution against throwing away the insights from traditional robotics. Things like safety guarantees, physical feasibility, and understanding why a system fails still matter a lot when you put a robot next to people. And many of the hard-won lessons, such as what makes a good state representation or how to handle uncertainty, are still very relevant, even if they now show up as inductive biases or architecture choices rather than hand-written equations.

So the relationship, to me, is complementary. Traditional robotics tells us what the structure of the problem looks like. Learning gives us the flexibility to handle the parts of the world we can't fully model. The most interesting research questions are at the intersection: where to put structure, and where to let data do the work.

r001.rationale: The response presents robot learning as extending robotics and handling parts of the same real-world tasks that traditional robotics addresses, describing the two as complementary.

r002.rationale: It notes a shift toward large-scale end-to-end learning, but explicitly rejects replacing traditional robotics methods and argues their insights remain important.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I actually don't see them as opposing camps, even though people sometimes frame it as "learning versus classical." I think of robot learning as building on top of everything traditional robotics figured out, not replacing it.

Traditional robotics gave us really powerful tools: kinematics, dynamics, control theory, motion planning, state estimation. Those things work beautifully when you can write down a precise model of the robot and the world. The problem is that for the environments we actually care about now, like a home or a hospital or a messy warehouse, you can't write down that model. There's too much variation in objects, in lighting, in how people interact with things. The classical pipeline tends to break at the perception and modeling stage, not at the control stage.

So that's where learning comes in. Learning is really good at the parts that are hard to specify by hand: understanding what's in a scene, inferring the state of a deformable object, figuring out the right contact strategy for grasping something you've never seen before. It's much less obvious that learning should replace a well-tuned low-level controller or a collision-checked planner, because those already work and come with guarantees that neural networks don't.

In my own work I think about it as a question of where to put the structure. If you have good priors from classical robotics, like the structure of a kinematic chain or the fact that tasks decompose into subgoals, you should use them. They make learning far more sample-efficient and more interpretable. Then you let data fill in the parts you genuinely don't know how to model. A lot of the best systems today look like that: a learned policy or perception module sitting inside a more traditional control and planning stack.

The thing I'd push back on is the idea that scaling data alone will make all of the classical stuff irrelevant. Robots are embodied, data is expensive, and safety matters. So I think the interesting research question for the next several years is not "learning or not," it's how the two fit together, and which abstractions let them talk to each other cleanly.

r001.rationale: The response describes how learning can complement traditional robotics, but it does not clearly state that both pursue the same underlying problems.

r002.rationale: The response explicitly rejects replacement: it presents learning as building on traditional robotics and says learning should not replace methods that already work.

astra-6.text:
I see robot learning as part of robotics, rather than something separate from traditional robotics. The goal is still to build machines that can perceive, reason, and act in the physical world. Learning gives us another set of tools for doing that.

Traditional robotics is very powerful when you can model the system and its environment well. You can use geometry, planning, and control to get precise, reliable behavior. But when a robot has to handle unfamiliar objects or operate in someone’s home, it becomes difficult to specify every situation by hand. That’s where learning can help: the robot can acquire behaviors or representations from data and experience.

The interesting question is how to combine these approaches. You might use learning for perception or to propose an action, while using a traditional controller to execute it. And knowledge about physics and geometry can make learning more efficient. So I think progress comes from understanding what each approach does well and building systems that bring them together.

r001.rationale: It says robot learning is part of robotics and shares the goal of building machines that perceive, reason, and act in the physical world.

r002.rationale: It presents learning as an additional set of tools to combine with geometry, planning, and control, not as replacing traditional methods with data-driven ones.

sol-6.1.text:
I see robot learning and traditional robotics as complementary. Traditional robotics gives us powerful tools for understanding the system: how a robot moves, how to control it, how to plan, and how to reason about physical constraints. Robot learning helps when parts of that system are difficult to model explicitly, like interpreting a cluttered scene or figuring out how to manipulate an unfamiliar object.

Take grasping, for example. You might learn from data where and how to grasp an object, but still use motion planning and feedback control to execute that grasp safely and accurately. Learning doesn’t mean we have to throw away everything we know about robotics.

The interesting question is where to put the boundary: what should we build into the system, and what should the robot learn from experience? I think a lot of progress comes from finding the right combination.

r001.rationale: The response describes robot learning and traditional robotics as complementary and says learning can help with difficult-to-model parts, but it does not state that both pursue the same underlying problems.

r002.rationale: The response explicitly says learning does not require throwing away existing robotics methods and gives grasping as a combination of learning, planning, and control, so it does not describe replacement by data-driven methods.
